quiz.q: What's the core difference between how Vec and HashMap find things?
options: Vec finds by key, HashMap finds by position
Vec finds by position (index), HashMap finds by a key you choose
There is no difference, they are interchangeable
HashMap can only store numbers
quiz.explain: Vec is ordered and positional (index 0, 1, 2...). HashMap looks values up by an arbitrary key you choose, like a name or id.

quiz.q: What happens when you `.insert()` a key into a HashMap that's already present?
options: It's a compile error
It panics at runtime
The old value is silently overwritten by the new one
Both values are kept in a list under that key
quiz.explain: insert() on an existing key replaces its value. A map holds each key exactly once. Check the Option returned by insert() if you need to know whether it overwrote something.

options: Always inserts 0, overwriting any existing count
Returns a mutable reference to the value for word, inserting 0 first only if the key was missing
Deletes the entry for word if it exists
Returns a copy of the value, not a reference
quiz.explain: entry().or_insert() is the one-lookup insert-or-update pattern: it gives you &mut V pointing at the (possibly newly-inserted) slot, so you can modify it directly, e.g. with *count += 1.

quiz.q: Why does `HashMap<Point, bool>` fail to compile if Point is a plain struct with no derives?
options: HashMap values must be primitives
Point needs Eq and Hash implementations so the map can hash it into a bucket and confirm key equality
Structs can never be used as generic parameters
bool cannot be a HashMap value type
quiz.explain: A HashMap key must be hashable (Hash) and comparable for equality (Eq) so lookups work. #[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash)] adds both automatically.

quiz.q: Why does deriving Hash on a struct also require deriving Eq (not just PartialEq)?
options: It doesn't — PartialEq alone is enough
Eq promises the equality check is total and reflexive, which the map relies on when confirming 'same hash bucket, so same key'
Eq makes hashing faster
Hash and Eq are unrelated and this is a coincidence
quiz.explain: Hash + Eq together let the map trust that two values hashing to the same bucket really are the same key when compared. PartialEq alone doesn't give that total-equality guarantee.

quiz.q: What does HashSet::insert(value) return, and what's it useful for?
options: Nothing (unit type)
true if the value was newly added, false if it was already present — useful for 'have I seen this before' checks
The number of elements now in the set
A reference to the inserted value
quiz.explain: The boolean return of insert() is what lets you write 'if seen.insert(word) { println!("new word") }' as a one-line first-sighting check.

quiz.q: Is HashMap iteration order guaranteed to match insertion order?
options: Yes, always
No — order is unspecified and can even change between runs of the same program
Only for HashMap<String, _>
Only if you call .sort() first
quiz.explain: Keys are scattered by hash for fast lookup, with no relation to insertion order, and Rust randomizes the hash seed per process as a DoS defense.

quiz.q: Which collection should you reach for when you need sorted iteration over key/value pairs?
options: HashMap, since it's the default
BTreeMap, which keeps keys in sorted order by design
Vec of tuples, always
HashSet
quiz.explain: HashMap makes no order guarantee. BTreeMap is built specifically to keep keys sorted at all times.

flashcards.front: Vec vs HashMap — how do they find elements?
flashcards.back: Vec finds by position (index). HashMap finds by an arbitrary key you choose.

flashcards.front: What does map.insert(k, v) do if k already exists?
flashcards.back: Overwrites the existing value silently. insert() returns Some(old_value) if it overwrote, None if the key was new.
map.entry(key).or_insert(default) returns &mut V to the slot, inserting default first only if missing — one lookup instead of get-then-insert.

flashcards.front: What traits does a custom struct need to be a HashMap key?
flashcards.back: #[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash)] — Eq for key equality checks, Hash for placing it in the right bucket.
A HashMap<T, ()> in spirit — tracks which keys/values exist with no attached value, for membership and uniqueness checks.

flashcards.front: What does HashSet::insert() return, and why is that useful?
flashcards.back: true if newly added, false if already present — lets you detect 'first time seeing this value' in one call.
No — unspecified, and can differ between runs of the same program due to per-process hash seed randomization.

flashcards.front: When should you use HashSet::contains vs Vec::contains?
flashcards.back: HashSet::contains is O(1) on average; Vec::contains scans linearly, O(n). Prefer HashSet for frequent membership checks.
